Issue Reading note
The gross-to-net series breaks on 1 January 2026 BMS cut the U.S. Eliquis list price roughly 40%. In Q2 2026 gross product sales declined 18% to $18,179M while net product sales rose 6% to $12,588M, and the gross-to-net adjustment moved from 46% to 30% (U.S. 52% to 34%). No gross-sales, rebate-ratio or average-net-price series spans 2025 and 2026 on one basis.
The latest full year is stale on three lines Against FY2025, Legacy ex-Eliquis is running at roughly half the rate ($941M in Q2 2026, −53% year over year), Eliquis has inflected up (+22%), and Opdivo has turned negative (−3%). Each is flagged where it bears on a section's conclusion.
GAAP earnings are inverted by deal accounting Acquired in-process R&D is expensed on closing: $12,533M in 2020 and $13,373M in 2024 produced GAAP diluted losses of $3.99 and $4.41 a share in otherwise profitable years. GAAP operating income, EBITDA and leverage cannot be trended without decomposing it. BMS reports no operating income line at all, so every operating-income figure here is constructed.
No franchise profitability exists One GAAP segment, consolidated net income as the CODM measure, and a three-way R&D split as the only segment expense disclosure. Every product or portfolio margin below is constructed. BMS also discloses no unit, prescription, patient-count, market-share or persistency metric for any product in any period.

1. Business description, model and unit economics

Bristol Myers Squibb sells patent-protected branded medicines, mostly injected or infused oncology biologics and oral specialty drugs, into the United States and about forty other markets. It does not sell to patients or to prescribers. It sells to three wholesalers who take title and resell within days, and the price it actually collects is set afterwards by rebate contracts with pharmacy benefit managers, by statutory formulas in Medicare and Medicaid, and since January 2026 by an administered price that the Department of Health and Human Services sets outright for selected products.▪ FY2025 gross product sales were $88,085M and net product sales $46,756M, a difference of $41,329M. Total revenues were $48,194M.

The company reports one GAAP segment. Management presents the business in MD&A as a Growth Portfolio and a Legacy Portfolio, which sorts products by growth rate rather than by remaining exclusivity. Eliquis is in the Legacy Portfolio and is treated separately here because its economics are unrelated to the genericising brands beside it: it is a 50/50 global alliance with Pfizer, and roughly half of Eliquis revenue goes to Pfizer under the revenue share.

Q2 2026 includes a $(9)M revenue-hedging contra line, so the three portfolios no longer sum to total revenue.)

What sets price. BMS does not set the price on its largest lines. U.S. gross-to-net adjustments were 53% of U.S. gross product sales in FY2025 against 49% in FY2024, on the January 2025 Medicare Part D redesign and a heavier government channel mix, and U.S. average net selling prices declined 4% in 2025 (FY2025 10-K, MD&A). Three of the six largest revenue lines are now on government-set U.S. prices with staggered start dates: Eliquis from 1 January 2026, Pomalyst from 1 January 2027, and Orencia selected in January 2026 for prices from 2028.▪ BMS challenged the statute, lost at the district court in April 2024 and at the Third Circuit in September 2025, and had certiorari denied in May 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026, Note 18). The remaining commercial lever is the list price itself, which BMS used in January 2026 and which is discussed below.

What drives volume. Volume moves product by product and does not aggregate into one exposure.

What drives cost. Very little of the reported cost of products sold is manufacturing. Of $13,936M in FY2025, $7,181M was payments to alliance partners, of which $6,980M was the Pfizer share of Eliquis, $742M was intangible impairment, inventory step-up and site-exit charges, and $505M was the Merck royalty on Reblozyl. What remains — roughly $5.5bn, about 11% of revenue — is the whole of BMS's physical cost of making medicine plus enterprise allocations (FY2025 10-K MD&A expense table and Note 3). The dominant cost in this business is the share of each franchise's economics that belongs to a partner, not manufacturing efficiency.

Gross-to-net by channel, duration of course, cost per unit and every implied patient count are [estimate: U.S. net revenue ÷ (list × (1 − channel gross-to-net)), with duration from clinical-practice norms]. The dominant sensitivity is duration: Opdivo at a twelve-month rather than a seven-month mean course moves implied patients from about 67,000 to about 39,000. The Reblozyl row is the most consequential. About 13,600 U.S. patients on therapy are inside a labelled population that the 10-K describes as transfusion-dependent anaemia from lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes and beta-thalassemia. Penetration of the currently labelled population is already high, and management's own pipeline slide dates the label-expansion readouts, in first-line non-transfusion-dependent MDS and in myelofibrosis, at 2027. Reblozyl's 31% FY2025 growth does not continue on penetration of the existing label.

Reconciling the build to reported cost: mAb and fusion-protein manufacturing at 12% of net sales on $20,404M of biologic revenue, autologous CAR-T at 48% on $1,785M, small molecules at 5% on $2,296M, plus the Merck royalty of $505M and an estimated Ono royalty, produces Growth Portfolio cost of products sold of roughly $5.0bn and a constructed Growth Portfolio gross margin of 80–84% [estimate: bottom-up cost build reconciled to reported COGS]. Adding constructed Eliquis and Legacy costs gives $13,245M against reported cost of products sold excluding specified items of $13,194M, a 0.4% overshoot. The range is wide because the Ono royalty is not disclosed and does not reconcile (see §5).

Eliquis. The economic unit is one 30-day equivalent supply of apixaban 5mg twice daily. Two independent angles were built to that unit: a Medicare Part D and MEPS build (52M units at $197 net) and a back-solve from the Q2 2026 gross-to-net reconciliation (58M units at $177 net). They differ by 12% on volume and 10% on price, which corroborates rather than conflicts.

Back-solving the Pfizer payment as half of net sales less cost of goods implies alliance cost of goods of 2.6% of net sales in FY2025, about $5 per 30-day equivalent. Generic apixaban 5mg by 56 tablets is listed in the UK Drug Tariff at £2.29–£2.80 in 2026, fully loaded with generic manufacturer and wholesaler margin, which scales to about $3.2 per 30-day equivalent [web]. Apixaban tablet cost is 2–3% of BMS's net revenue per unit and drives nothing. The entire cost structure of this franchise is the 48.3% paid to Pfizer plus BMS's own undisclosed selling cost.▪ A per-unit international build cannot be constructed even at Tier 2: neither partner discloses country price or volume, the country mix changes every year as generics enter individual markets, and European reference pricing sets a different price per country.

At an API cost ten-fold above the upper bound, Revlimid's variable margin is still 94%. Reported gross margin for this segment is lower than the variable margin because reported product cost includes proportionate allocations of enterprise-wide facilities and information-technology cost that do not leave when the product does. It is 90–96% on a four-year mix reconciliation [estimate: four-year gross-profit mix residual] and 67–72% on a single quarter, because quarterly cost of products sold absorbs impairments and allocations that do not scale with a collapsing product. Variable contribution margin is roughly 95–98% and reported margin is in the high eighties to mid nineties, trending down as the allocation base shrinks.▪

Growth Portfolio growth against company revenue. Growth Portfolio revenue rose $9,652M between 2022 and 2025. Roughly 60% of that came from a $7.6bn block that is 15.8% of company revenue, and roughly 28% came from a $14.4bn block whose principal patent expires in 2028. At company level the two portfolios almost exactly cancelled, leaving revenue excluding Eliquis 1.2% higher in 2025 than in 2020 (§6).

1.3 The 2026 price reset, and why it raised realised price

BMS cut the U.S. Eliquis list price from $606 to $346 per 30-day supply effective 1 January 2026, at the same moment the IRA maximum fair price of $231 took effect and the $0 Medicaid arrangement began. Reported U.S. Eliquis revenue rose 26.5% in Q2 2026. U.S. volume cannot plausibly have risen more than high single digits, because new-to-brand share moved only from approximately 75% to approaching 80% across three quarters and the treated population grows with the 65+ cohort at roughly 3% a year. Net price per 30-day equivalent therefore rose roughly 18–23% in the first quarter of government price-setting while list price declined 43%▪ [estimate: reported U.S. revenue growth less bounded volume growth].

Both the Medicaid unit rebate amount and the IRA inflation rebate are computed as current AMP less a base-date AMP escalated by CPI-U. Cutting AMP reduces that penalty dollar for dollar, and since 1 January 2024 the 100%-of-AMP cap no longer limits the Medicaid rebate.▪ Eliquis's WAC compounded at about 6.0% a year from 2018 to 2024 against much lower CPI-U [web], so thirteen years of accumulated penalty were removed at once. Management described the same thing commercially: "The roughly 40% WAC reduction eliminates the inflationary penalties or CPI penalties of statutory rebates that have been accumulating over many years for the brand" (Q4 2025 earnings call).

Sizing it: guidance of +20% to +25% on a $14,443M base is $2,889M to $3,611M of incremental revenue, roughly $1.4–1.9bn of incremental BMS gross profit at a 48–52% retained margin, and $0.56 to $0.75 of EPS at the guided 18% tax rate over roughly 2,040M diluted shares — about 9% to 12% of the $6.05–6.35 initial 2026 guidance [estimate: guided growth × constructed retained margin]. That is what a single administrative price reset on one product produced, two years before that product loses U.S. exclusivity.

The reset is revenue-accretive and cash-dilutive in the transition year. H1 2026 operating cash flow was $4,497M against $5,871M, and the 10-Q attributes the $1.4bn decline to "lower net customer receipts, primarily due to a list price reduction for [Eliquis]." Rebates accrued on 2025 gross-priced sales are still being paid out against 2026 receipts struck at the lower gross price.

1.4 Contract structure

There is no backlog, no take-or-pay, no escalator and no renewal term anywhere in this business. The 10-K states that "customer orders are generally fulfilled within a few days of receipt resulting in minimal order backlog." Payment terms run 30 to 90 days. The only durable contracts are the distribution service agreements with the three wholesalers, which all expire in June 2027, and the alliance agreements on the supply side. Revenue persistence comes from patients staying on therapy and from formulary position, both of which reset annually.

Operating leverage is not visible at consolidated level, and the reason is arithmetic rather than cost discipline. A 57.6% increase in Growth Portfolio revenue between 2022 and 2025 produced a 4.4% increase in consolidated revenue, because the mix moved simultaneously out of Revlimid at roughly 96% gross margin and into both Eliquis at roughly 49% and the Growth Portfolio at roughly 81%. The FY2025 operating expense reduction of $1.2bn came from the $2.0bn strategic productivity initiative, of which about $1bn was banked in 2025, not from volume.

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

Bristol Myers Squibb's competitive advantage is based on granted patents, regulatory exclusivity and a large payer-facing commercial organisation.▪ Every material product line in the FY2025 revenue base is assigned a dated exclusivity estimate rather than a technical barrier a competitor cannot cross. FY2025 revenue by the origin of the technology:

Origin Products FY2025 revenue % of $48,194M
Internal BMS discovery Eliquis, Orencia, Sprycel, Sotyktu $18,932M 39.3%
Internal, excluding Eliquis Orencia, Sprycel, Sotyktu $4,489M 9.3%
Medarex (2009, $2.4bn [web]) Opdivo, Qvantig, Yervoy, Opdualag $14,372M 29.8%
Celgene (2019) Revlimid, Pomalyst, Reblozyl, Breyanzi, Zeposia, Abecma, Abraxane $10,741M 22.3%
MyoKardia (2020, $13.1bn) Camzyos $1,068M 2.2%
Mirati (2024, $4.8bn) Krazati $205M 0.4%
Karuna (2024, $14.0bn) Cobenfy $155M 0.3%

On any reasonable attribution, internally discovered technology outside Eliquis is under 10% of revenue.▪ Two capabilities do differentiate technically, and both are narrower than the slides suggest.

Autologous CAR-T manufacturing at commercial scale is the strongest technical evidence in the company. Breyanzi launched third to market and spent three years vector-constrained, and became the largest CD19 CAR-T in the world by worldwide sales in Q3 2025 with manufacturing success rates management describes as "in the 90s" and roughly 13,000 patients treated across the franchise (shareholder and analyst call, 2025-12-11; Bernstein conference, 2025-09-23). Breyanzi U.S. revenue rose 68% and international 132% in FY2025, and the product reached $484M in Q2 2026 against Gilead's entire cell-therapy line of $417M. Management attributes the win to the combination of efficacy, safety, label breadth and manufacturing rather than to manufacturing alone, and the label evidence supports that: Breyanzi is approved in LBCL, FL, CLL/SLL, MCL and MZL while Yescarta's label is narrower. Abecma is the counter-example on the same technology: its U.S. revenue declined 14% in 2025 "primarily due to lower demand from increased competition in BCMA targeted therapies," and J&J and Legend's Carvykti posted $657M in Q2 2026 alone [web], larger than Abecma's entire FY2025 of $427M. Manufacturing capability did not save the weaker construct. The substitution threat is in vivo CAR-T, which removes apheresis and the cell-therapy centre entirely; BMS bought it rather than waiting for it, paying $1,700M for Orbital Therapeutics in December 2025 with $1,379M expensed immediately, for a preclinical lead asset.

The cereblon and CELMoD chemistry library inherited with Celgene is the second. CELMoDs bind cereblon, the substrate receptor of the CRL4 E3 ubiquitin ligase, and reshape its surface so a protein with no druggable pocket is recruited, ubiquitinated and destroyed. It reaches targets small-molecule inhibition cannot; the Chief Medical Officer put it plainly on the Q2 2026 call about BCL-6, "because it's the [transcription] factor, we were unable to inhibit them. Now with the degrader we can." The barrier is a proprietary chemical library plus the proteomics to identify which substrates a new chemotype recruits, and Celgene spent a decade building it. Seven years after the acquisition it has produced no revenue. The first commercial CELMoD is iberdomide, with a PDUFA date of 17 August 2026; mezigdomide's is 13 May 2027.

Everything else labelled a platform was purchased. §11 scores what they produced. Four platform acquisitions closing between January 2024 and December 2025 committed $24,648M of headline consideration, plus $2,550M of upfronts and milestones already paid to BioNTech and SystImmune; together they produced $360M of FY2025 revenue and $118M in Q2 2026.

PD-1 and CTLA-4 checkpoint inhibition is not hard to replicate, and the proof is that a competitor replicated it faster and better. At least eight PD-(L)1 agents are marketed globally and biosimilar development is underway ahead of the 2028 U.S. composition-of-matter expiry. Merck's pembrolizumab reached $31,680M of 2025 sales against Opdivo's $10,049M. In 2017 BMS and Ono licensed the antibody patents to Merck for $625M plus a royalty of 6.5% of worldwide Keytruda sales through 2023 and 2.5% from 2024 through 2026 [web]. The intellectual property was worth more as a legal claim than as a commercial advantage. BMS booked $588M of Keytruda royalty income in 2025 and the stream terminates on 31 December 2026. BMS also pays Ono 4% in North America and 15% elsewhere on nivolumab, so the economics of its largest franchise are shared upstream on a technology it did not originate.

The live substitution threat to that franchise is the PD-(L)1 × VEGF bispecific class. At ASCO 2026, HARMONi-6 reported ivonescimab plus chemotherapy against a PD-1 plus chemotherapy control in first-line squamous NSCLC with median overall survival of 27.9 against 23.7 months and a 34% reduction in death risk [web]. BMS's answer is to rent one: pumitamig, licensed from BioNTech in June 2025 for $1.5bn upfront, $2.0bn of non-contingent anniversary payments across 2026–2028, up to $7.6bn of milestones and an equal global profit share. The incumbent with roughly a fifth of class revenue is paying $3.5bn of guaranteed cash for a partner's next-generation molecule.▪

Subcutaneous checkpoint inhibition shows that formulation science does not differentiate in this class. Opdivo Qvantig co-formulates nivolumab with Halozyme's recombinant hyaluronidase, converting a 30-minute infusion into a three-minute injection. Neither company owns the mechanism: Merck's Keytruda Qlex uses Alteogen's enzyme and was approved on 19 September 2025 [web]. BMS launched three quarters earlier and reached 15% U.S. franchise share with revenue annualising above $1bn by Q2 2026; Merck, two quarters after approval, reported Qlex sales of $463M with double-digit adoption of the U.S. Keytruda business and the same 30–40% target by end-2027 [web]. Nine months of lead time left BMS at $261M of Q2 2026 Qvantig revenue against Merck's $463M. It also does not extend the patent: footnote (g) to the FY2025 exclusivity table assigns Qvantig U.S. 2028 and EU 2030, the same dates as IV Opdivo, "based on the expiry of the COM patent for nivolumab and does not include any potential exclusivity resulting from pending patent applications relating to Opdivo Qvantig."

  • Sotyktu. Sotyktu's allosteric TYK2 inhibition is internally discovered medicinal chemistry — binding the pseudokinase regulatory domain rather than the ATP site is what allows selectivity and avoids the JAK-class boxed warning — and it has been beaten head to head on its own mechanism: in the 606-patient Phase 3 LATITUDE Atlas study Takeda's zasocitinib achieved PASI 100 above 35% at week 16 against approximately 14% for deucravacitinib, with statistical superiority on all key secondary endpoints [web].
  • Camzyos. Cardiac myosin inhibition treats the disease mechanism rather than the symptoms, and Camzyos has the second-longest exclusivity in the portfolio, U.S. 2036 with patent-term restoration granted and EU 2038 with SPCs granted in France, Germany, Italy and Spain, behind Krazati at 2037. Cytokinetics' aficamten was approved on 19 December 2025 and available in the U.S. from late January 2026, competing on monitoring burden rather than efficacy.
  • Actinium-225. Radiopharmaceutical therapy is bound by a physical input constraint rather than by intellectual property: RayzeBio paused Phase 3 ACTION-1 enrolment in 2024 because it could not secure enough actinium-225 [web], BMS paid $4,147M for the platform, and it has generated no revenue. BMS opened a U.S. radiopharmaceutical hub in Indianapolis in 2025 able to deliver doses within three days of production. Isotope allocation, not science, determines whether the platform scales.

Shipping the roadmap. BMS has missed more of its stated dates in the last twelve months than before. The 2023 R&D Day set three productivity targets — roughly ten INDs a year, a first-in-human-to-approval success rate of about 20%, and a median 6.5 years from first-in-human to approval. No subsequent deck or call reports against any of them.▪ On the Q2 2026 call the milvexian and Cobenfy ADEPT readouts both slipped into 2027 (§7). Subcutaneous nivolumab is the one large roadmap item BMS shipped on schedule, and the commercial claim attached to it narrowed along the way, from covering "up to 75% of the indications" with "about half of that business" convertible in January 2024 to a flat 30–40% of the IV business from Q4 2024 onward.

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

Bristol Myers Squibb earns excess returns today and will keep earning them for about three more years, and it does not hold a durable competitive advantage. What it holds is a set of granted patents with disclosed expiry dates, and 65.0% of FY2025 revenue comes from products whose exclusivity ends between November 2026 and December 2028.▪ BMS has no switching cost, no unit-cost gap that widens with volume and no network effect, and its regulatory position works against it. The 10-K says: "Upon the expiration or loss of market exclusivity on a product, we can lose the major portion of that product's revenue in a very short period of time," and it names as its competitive factors "product efficacy, safety and ease of use, price and demonstrated cost-effectiveness, marketing effectiveness, product labeling, customer service and R&D of new products."

BMS earns excess returns while the patents run. It spends 20.6% of revenue on R&D and a further $3.7bn on acquired in-process R&D just to hold position, and its FY2025 ROIC of 15.5% ranks eighth of the ten large-cap biopharma peers computed here; against that, a constructed Growth Portfolio gross margin of 80–84%, a consolidated free-cash-flow margin of 26.7% and 17% Growth Portfolio growth are real excess returns.

Management claims: the 10-K says its long-term position "depends upon our success in discovering and developing innovative, cost-effective products." The investor-facing framing is stronger, "industry-leading sustainable growth into the 2030s and beyond" (JPM, 2026-01-12), and it depends on a pipeline that has not yet produced revenue. Both can be true only if the pipeline delivers, which is a forecast rather than an advantage.

External sources: Merck's own FY2025 10-K books $525M of Reblozyl alliance revenue against BMS's $2,327M of Reblozyl sales, 22.6% of the top line, consistent with the 20–24% tiered royalty BMS discloses and confirming that the fastest-growing large Growth franchise gives away more than a fifth of revenue before manufacturing. And Cytokinetics' aficamten was approved in December 2025 for the same indication as Camzyos, four years into a patent that runs to 2036. The one clear positive: BMS is converting to subcutaneous faster than Merck, at 9.5% of the worldwide franchise and 12.7% in the U.S. in Q2 2026 measured on disclosed revenue (management states about 15% U.S. conversion) against Keytruda Qlex at 5.5% and 7.9%, though part of that gap is a nine-month launch lead.

Ground-up view: in this industry excess returns accrue to whoever holds an unexpired patent on a clinically differentiated molecule. Minimum efficient scale in discovery is high but not prohibitive, and the evidence is that BMS's own newest molecules were bought from Karuna, Mirati, MyoKardia, Celgene, BioNTech and SystImmune, companies with a fraction of its R&D budget. If scale in discovery conferred an advantage, the pipeline would be internally sourced.▪ Switching costs are effectively zero for the large franchises, because oncology regimens are set by guidelines and trial data and a payer formulary exclusion "can lead to sharply reduced usage." The two places where something like a switching cost exists — the Camzyos REMS programme and certified CAR-T treatment centres — together covered $2,853M, 10.8% of the Growth Portfolio, and one of them lost 11 points of BCMA share in a single year despite site qualification.

3.2 Return on invested capital

ROIC is NOPAT — constructed operating income taxed at BMS's own 17% non-GAAP effective rate, the reported rate being unusable because acquired IPRD is largely non-deductible and 2020 and 2024 were pretax losses — over average invested capital of total debt plus BMS shareholders' equity less cash and marketable debt securities.

Standalone: ROIC was 23.6% in 2017 and 39.9% in 2018 on $10–14bn of invested capital. Post-Celgene it has earned 9.0% to 15.5% on $52–82bn. The $80,269M of total consideration transferred for Celgene more than doubled revenue and cut the return on capital by roughly two thirds.▪ The two rolling three-year windows that span the deal put the incremental return at 1.8% (2016 to 2019) and 3.6% (2018 to 2021); from 2019 onward invested capital declines every year as acquired intangibles amortise faster than new deals replace them, so the ratio takes a negative denominator and stops being interpretable. $32,514M of acquired IPRD was expensed between 2020 and 2025 and never entered invested capital, while the intangibles that did enter amortise away; capitalising cumulative acquired IPRD back into invested capital puts FY2025 ROIC at 9.8% rather than 15.5%, and shrinks the 2021-to-2025 improvement from 6.5 points to 2.2. NOPAT was $8,169M in FY2021 and $8,486M in FY2025, up 3.9% over four years, against $31,220M of cash paid for acquisitions in FY2022–FY2025 and $18,007M of acquired IPRD expensed in FY2023–FY2025. Roughly $49bn of gross deployment bought a 3.9% increase in NOPAT.▪ Free cash flow margin has held 26–33% every year since 2020.

The products driving Growth Portfolio expansion — Reblozyl at a 20–24% royalty to Merck, Breyanzi as autologous CAR-T, Opdivo and Yervoy paying Ono — have structurally worse unit economics than the products they are replacing, which were wholly owned oral small molecules. Mix shift into the Growth Portfolio is dilutive to gross margin, which is the opposite of what a strengthening advantage looks like.▪

For the Legacy Portfolio excluding Eliquis there is no durable advantage. What produced excess returns there was a legal monopoly, and it has expired: the FY2025 exclusivity table marks Revlimid, Pomalyst, Sprycel and Abraxane with a footnote flag rather than a date in the U.S., EU and Japan; the footnotes say generics have entered for Revlimid, Sprycel and Abraxane, and for Pomalyst that U.S. generic entry was expected in the first quarter of 2026, which it then was. The volume-cap schedule inside Celgene's settlement licences was a private contract that ceased to bind on 31 January 2026. The Lenalidomide REMS is a shared-system programme that covers generic lenalidomide alongside the brand, and six filers cleared it, so it is a toll rather than a barrier. Revlimid's acquired product right was fully amortised in Q4 2024 and Pomalyst's in Q4 2025, so any return-on-capital measure on this book now divides a shrinking profit by an invested-capital base of approximately zero.

Management's own two rules for slower erosion both failed inside its own portfolio. The 10-K states that drugs more complex to manufacture, such as sterile injectables, usually decline more slowly, and that specialty drugs decline more slowly than primary-care drugs. Abraxane, a protein-bound sterile injectable, declined 78% in the U.S. in FY2025, faster than Revlimid, an oral capsule, at 49%. Sprycel, a specialty oncology oral, lost 70% of U.S. revenue in its first full year after generic entry. Revlimid's slower path is explained by the volume caps, not by the setting.

Eliquis is its own case and does not fit that middle description either. The advantage came from the trial result: ARISTOTLE, in 18,201 patients, showed apixaban reduced stroke or systemic embolism 21%, major bleeding 31% and all-cause mortality 11% versus warfarin, the only oral anticoagulant to win on all three [web]. Fifteen years of prescribing habit built on that result produced roughly 75–80% U.S. new-prescription share and the number-one oral anticoagulant position globally. But it cannot survive its own expiry date, which is close. Apixaban is a small-molecule tablet dispensed through a pharmacy benefit, so substitution at the counter is automatic once an AB-rated product exists; there is no device, no formulation barrier and no manufacturing scale barrier of the kind that slowed Humira's biosimilars. And BMS keeps roughly half: over 2016–2025 it booked $94,283M of Eliquis revenue and paid Pfizer $44,963M, 47.7% of every revenue dollar, a ratio that has never moved outside 47.0–48.3% in ten years and has moved against BMS.▪ The Pfizer share alone consumed 14.5 points of consolidated FY2025 gross margin.

The two partners also disclose the expiry date differently, and the difference is material. BMS's exclusivity table says U.S. 2028, with a footnote that settled generic companies "are permitted to launch in 2028, subject to additional challenges." Pfizer's FY2025 10-K adds that the three companies that litigated to judgment cannot launch until a formulation patent expires in 2031, and that if that formulation patent is held invalid or not infringed on appeal, the settled generics "would be permitted to launch on November 21, 2026," or immediately if both patents fall. Azurity filed a 505(b)(2) with a paragraph IV certification against exactly that formulation patent in November 2025. BMS discloses 2028. Pfizer discloses 21 November 2026 to 2031 on the same asset.

Business-model analogues. The closest public comparison is Gilead Sciences: a portfolio that depends on a small number of molecules with defined expiry dates, replenished by large M&A with a mixed record, earning a high gross margin (78.8%) on low growth (3.6% five-year CAGR) and a low-twenties ROIC. It breaks in one place, because Gilead's HIV base has an unusually long tail and BMS has no single asset of comparable durability. Amgen is the second: a biologics portfolio with a serial loss-of-exclusivity cadence, a comparable gross margin and the same dependence on large deals to refill the pipeline; it breaks because Amgen's biosimilar unit gives it a second, structurally different earnings stream. Merck & Co. is the same shape one notch stronger, an oncology franchise on a dated patent expiry, far more concentrated at 48.7% of revenue in Keytruda and earning a materially better return at 24.7% ROIC. For the Eliquis franchise specifically the analogue is AbbVie's Humira, a single dominant brand at 35–40% of revenue with a clinical-superiority origin and a death date the market knows years ahead; it breaks because AbbVie owned all of Humira's economics and entered its cliff with Skyrizi and Rinvoq already at $9,577M of U.S. revenue, while BMS owns half of Eliquis and its designated successor is still blinded.

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

Inside the Growth Portfolio, BMS is the scale leader in exactly one business line, and it is materially sub-scale in most of the others. Breyanzi's $484M in Q2 2026 exceeded Gilead's entire cell-therapy franchise of $417M for the first time. In checkpoint inhibitors it is a durable but shrinking number two, at 20.8% of the four-player pool with clean USD filing disclosure against Merck's 64.0%, down from 23.0% in FY2023.▪ In immunology it is not a factor: $4,573M against AbbVie's $25,866M of Skyrizi plus Rinvoq. In BCMA cell therapy it went from 29.7% to 18.5% of a two-player market in one year. In neuroscience it is running at roughly one-sixth of the revenue rate J&J's Caplyta reached from a similarly priced acquisition made a year later. The competitor closing fastest is AstraZeneca, whose Imfinzi compounded at 19.6% a year over FY2023–FY2025 and grew 31% in H1 2026 against the Opdivo family's 6.9% two-year rate.▪

Cobenfy is the sharpest comparison in the portfolio: two neuropsychiatry acquisitions of near-identical price made a year apart, with Caplyta running at 5.7x Cobenfy's revenue rate. BMS's own diagnosis on the Q2 2026 call was that prescribing behaviour is deeply entrenched and that it needs to "accelerate new patient starts as well as improve repeat prescribing." In KRAS, only $640M of the $4,801M Mirati price was allocated to Krazati's marketed rights and $3.5bn went to in-process R&D, so that transaction is a pipeline bet with a small commercial asset attached, and Krazati's scale should be judged on that basis.

4.5 Oral anticoagulation — Eliquis

Here BMS is the scale leader by a wide and still-widening margin: about 79.5% of U.S. branded direct-oral-anticoagulant revenue and roughly two-thirds of the branded market globally.▪

Herfindahl on U.S. branded DOAC revenue is about 6,700: one dominant seller and one distant second. The competitive threat is the April 2028 U.S. patent date and the November 2026 EU expiry. Generic rivaroxaban is a smaller threat than it looks: twelve ANDA holders have FDA approval across all strengths, but CMS's acquisition-cost file shows a generic price only for the 2.5mg strength and the paediatric suspension as of 22 July 2026, while the 10mg, 15mg and 20mg tablets that account for the atrial-fibrillation and VTE volume remain brand-only at $19.54 per 20mg tablet. An asymmetry runs the other way from 2027: CMS removed Xarelto from the negotiation programme effective 1 January 2027 after determining a generic is being bona fide marketed, so Xarelto's U.S. net price will no longer be administratively set while Eliquis remains under its maximum fair price, and Eliquis has no equivalent route out before April 2028.

The January 2026 price inversion is the structural fact of this market right now, and CMS's survey-based acquisition-cost file captures it without any company framing:

Through December 2025 the two leading DOACs were at effective parity on daily acquisition cost. Since January 2026 Eliquis has cost 43% less per day than Xarelto at the pharmacy counter. The clinically preferred agent is now also the lower-priced one.

4.6 The genericising book — where BMS is no longer the scale leader in anything

In a genericised molecule the scale-defining metric is share of dispensed volume and the number of marketing suppliers, because those two set price. CMS Medicare Part D and Part B data, pulled 2026-08-08, gives both.

Line BMS brand First U.S. generic Suppliers marketing, 2026 Q1 BMS share of molecule claims Generic price against brand, per claim
Lenalidomide Revlimid March 2022 (volume-limited licences) 15 91.1% (2022), 54.8% (2024), 32.0% (2025), 15.7% (2026 Q1) 77% (2022–24), 69% (2025), 54% (2026 Q1)
Pomalidomide Pomalyst 2 March 2026 6 100% (2025), 85.2% (2026 Q1), and roughly two-thirds of March-only claims 55% in the first month
Dasatinib Sprycel September 2024 9 87.6% (2024), 21.0% (2025), 12.0% (2026 Q1) 68% (2024), 57% (2025), 40% (2026 Q1)
nab-paclitaxel Abraxane April 2022 (505(b)(2)); October 2024 (first ANDA) not separable within one HCPCS code U.S. revenue $541M (2024), $116M (2025), $48M annualising Part B $2,905 per claim (2025), $1,923 (2026 Q1)

Molecule demand is not falling. Medicare lenalidomide claims grew from 361,641 in 2022 to 468,173 in 2025, and Q1 2026 annualises to 474,944; dasatinib claims grew from 44,274 in 2024 to 64,333 in 2025; nab-paclitaxel Part B claims rose 15% in 2025. Every dollar BMS lost went to a competitor at a lower price, not to a shrinking patient population, so there is no volume recovery to model.▪ The contractual caps held the generic price as well as the generic volume. Generic lenalidomide was priced at a 23% discount to brand across 2022, 2023 and 2024 while the licences were volume-limited, widened to 31% in 2025, and went to 46% in the single quarter after the caps lapsed, with the manufacturer count moving from 11 to 14. The two entrants that arrived uncapped priced at $5,280 and $6,942 per claim against the licensed incumbents' $9,100–10,700. A generic whose volume is contractually capped has little reason to discount.

Brand price never eroded through any of it. Revlimid's gross Part D price per claim was $16,237 in 2020, $18,022 in 2022, $17,426 in 2024 and $17,601 in Q1 2026, roughly flat across the whole generic period, while brand claims went from 344,297 in 2021 to 18,678 in Q1 2026. The revenue decline is volume. BMS's MD&A separately attributes part of the FY2025 decline to lower average net selling prices, and both statements are true because they measure different things: gross list price is a BMS decision and net price is set by the channel, which the Part D redesign moved against BMS in 2025.

Class displacement is happening independently of generics. Aggregating the CMS myeloma pool, BMS's branded book (Revlimid, Pomalyst, Empliciti, Thalomid, Abecma) was 36.9% of the identified U.S. Medicare pool in 2025 and is 27.4% annualising Q1 2026, while J&J's Darzalex, Carvykti, Tecvayli and Talvey went from 28.3% to 33.6%. The lead in branded U.S. Medicare myeloma changed hands. In CML, Novartis lost Tasigna to generics (18.2% to 7.0% of the Part D pool) and Scemblix more than replaced it (20.7% to 30.8%), so Novartis's branded position, including Gleevec, held at roughly 41% (41.9% to 40.6%) while Sprycel's went from 7.4% to 4.4%. That is the lifecycle manoeuvre BMS is attempting in myeloma with iberdomide and mezigdomide, executed by a competitor.

5. Value chain and profit pools

The dollar decomposition below starts from $100 of U.S. list-price spend on a BMS medicine in FY2025. BMS discloses the U.S. and non-U.S. gross-to-net rates but not the U.S. gross-sales dollars, so the split is reconstructed: U.S. net product sales of about $33.0bn at a 53% rate implies U.S. gross of about $71.0bn, non-U.S. gross about $17.1bn, and the two sum to the disclosed $88,085M after a 1.0% scaling [estimate: region table less in-region alliance revenue, grossed at the disclosed rates].

Of the $53 that leaves BMS's U.S. list price, roughly $25 goes to government programmes, $19 to contracted purchasers through chargebacks, and $8 to commercial payers and PBMs. The three wholesalers that physically move 87–90% of the product keep about $1 of operating profit, the smallest slice of any named layer. The profit pool is at BMS and at the contracted purchasers.▪

Distribution is the thinnest-margin layer in the chain. McKesson's North American Pharmaceutical segment earned $3,658M of operating profit on $336,652M of revenue (1.09%); Cencora's U.S. Healthcare Solutions earned $3,575M on roughly $291bn (1.2%); Cardinal's Pharma segment earned $2,258M on $204,644M (1.10%). Their combined operating profit on all U.S. drug distribution — every manufacturer's product, not just BMS's — is $9,491M, about the same as BMS's own $9,328M of pretax income, on a revenue base seventeen times larger. Their own customer concentration is worse than BMS's supplier concentration: CVS Health alone is 24% of McKesson's revenue and 30% of Cardinal's, Walgreens and Boots are 25% of Cencora's, and Cardinal lost the OptumRx contract, 17% of revenue, outright in June 2024. The entity with pricing power over the distribution layer is the PBM-owned pharmacy chain, not the wholesaler.

The chargeback layer is the largest single non-government claimant on the U.S. brand dollar, and its growth is disconnected from patient demand. BMS discloses charge-backs and cash discounts of $14,067M in FY2025, up 22% on 5% gross-sales growth, without breaking out the 340B share. Industry-wide, 340B purchases reached $100.0bn in 2025, up 22.8%, with $79.5bn of discount value available to covered entities, against total U.S. manufacturer gross-to-net reductions of $416bn [web]. On the same source, only three of eight large manufacturers disclose an average list-to-net discount for 2025; BMS is at −53% against −49% in 2024, in the middle of a three-company range running from −46% to −56% with an unweighted average of −51.7%. That is not an outlier, and it is consistent with a portfolio unusually exposed to Medicare.

Patent expiry and statute are the binding constraints, not the channel. Physical distribution is concentrated but not scarce: the distribution service agreements cap wholesaler inventory at no more than one month of demand, BMS disclosed no product above one month on hand at 30 June 2026, and the June 2027 expiry is a fee renegotiation rather than a supply risk. Manufacturing is a constraint in only two small pockets, both named in Item 1 — CAR-T viral vector, where BMS says it is "accelerating our plans to transition to new vector technologies with a dual sourcing strategy," and radiopharmaceutical isotopes — together covering $1,785M, 3.7% of FY2025 revenue. Two things constrain the business instead: patent expiry limits the volume the company is allowed to sell, and statute sets the price on the largest lines. Eliquis, Pomalyst and Orencia were $20,881M, 43% of FY2025 revenue, and all three are now on or scheduled for administratively set U.S. prices.▪

Alliance payments rose from $4,169M in 2019 to $7,181M in 2025, on terms fixed at signing. They are inside cost of products sold. Pfizer alone went from 10.9% of BMS total revenue in 2021 to 14.5% in 2025, and total alliance payments were 17.0% of revenue in Q2 2026. It is the arithmetic of a fixed profit share on the one large product that kept growing while the rest of the portfolio shrank. BMS's contractual commitments also run upstream rather than downstream: $18.3bn of potential contingent R&D milestones ($9.6bn pre-Phase-III, $8.7bn post-Phase-III), $21.5bn of sales-based milestones, and $2.0bn of non-contingent BioNTech anniversary payments across 2026–2028. There is no corresponding downstream take-or-pay; customers commit to nothing beyond a purchase order.

Circularity: BMS collects royalties from its two largest immuno-oncology competitors, and they stop at the end of 2026. Pretax income from royalties was approximately $2.7 billion in 2025 against pretax income of $9,328M, 29% of the total, and most of it is outside revenue in Other (income)/expense. The Q2 2026 10-Q already shows divestiture royalty income of $0 for the six months against $558M a year earlier. The Merck relationship runs both ways in the same year: BMS paid Merck $505M of Reblozyl royalties and received $289M of Winrevair royalties in 2025.

The rebate float is a $10.6bn interest-free loan from the channel, and it is unwinding. The gross-to-net reserve was $10,565M at 31 December 2025 on $88,085M of gross product sales, roughly 94 days of gross-to-net payments. Cutting the list price destroys the float: accrued rebates and discounts went from $8,844M at 31 December 2025 to $5,654M at 30 June 2026, with a matching $3,135M cash outflow in the half.▪ Near-term available cash is roughly $3bn below what FY2025's $14.2bn of operating cash flow implies.

6. Secular and industry trends

Management's claimed secular driver is the Growth Portfolio. It compounded at 15.9% over 2020–2025 while company revenue excluding Eliquis rose 1.2% in total.

Growth attribution. Over 2020–2025 the Growth Portfolio grew from roughly $12,623M to $26,409M, a 15.9% compound rate adding $13,786M, while Legacy ex-Eliquis declined from $20,780M to $7,342M, subtracting $13,438M. The two almost exactly cancelled. Total revenue rose $5,676M, a 2.5% compound rate, and $5,275M of that — 93% — was Eliquis. Excluding Eliquis, revenue was $33,350M in 2020 and $33,751M in 2025: 1.2% cumulative over five years, 0.24% a year.▪

Acquisitions contributed little, which cuts in management's favour. Products BMS did not own in 2020 contributed at least $1,428M of FY2025 revenue (Camzyos $1,068M, Krazati $205M, Cobenfy $155M, plus Augtyro inside an undisclosed line), so organic FY2025 revenue is about $46.8bn against a $42,518M base, a 1.9% compound rate. Acquisitions supplied roughly 25% of total growth and about 10% of the Growth Portfolio's gain. The Growth Portfolio build is overwhelmingly internal or previously in-licensed rather than bought.

Against the peer growth cohort, BMS is last. Every named large-cap pharma peer grew faster over the five-year window, and every one except Pfizer, whose COVID unwind dominates the shorter comparison, grew faster over the three-year window.

Management's own defence is the loss-of-exclusivity cohort. AbbVie absorbed a larger single-product loss over a shorter window and still compounded at 6.0%: Humira went from $14,404M to $4,540M globally over 2023–2025, a $9,864M loss, while Skyrizi plus Rinvoq went from $11,732M to $25,866M, a 143% replacement ratio. BMS's own two-year ratio is 114% and its five-year ratio is 103%, which left Eliquis as the sole source of net growth.▪ Skyrizi alone was $17,562M in 2025; BMS's largest non-Opdivo Growth Portfolio product is Orencia at $3,705M, which is flat and IRA-selected for 2028.

BMS compounded at 2.5% against a market compounding at 5–8%. IQVIA's 2026 forecast puts global medicine spending at approximately $2.6 trillion by 2030 at a 5–8% CAGR, with U.S. net price growth of 4–7% through 2030 after a 9.4% net CAGR over the past five years, and brand losses from patent expiries of nearly $200 billion through 2030, "larger than the one the industry navigated in 2011 and 2012" [web]. In oncology, where it is most concentrated, global cancer-medicine spending was $252bn in 2024 and grew an average 11.9% a year over 2020–2024. BMS's oncology and haematology revenue was approximately $27.9bn in 2020 and approximately $25.2bn in 2025 [estimate: BMS oncology defined as the Opdivo family plus Yervoy, Reblozyl, Breyanzi, Abecma, Krazati, Revlimid, Pomalyst, Sprycel and Abraxane; the market base is back-solved from IQVIA's 2024 level and stated growth; IQVIA measures list prices while BMS books net, so the level of implied share is overstated in both years and the decline is somewhat smaller than the raw arithmetic suggests].

The share loss is almost entirely mechanical. It is patent expiry on Revlimid, Pomalyst, Sprycel and Abraxane, not competitive displacement in the products BMS still sells. Within checkpoint inhibitors it lost about two points of class share over two years and regained ground in 2025. Within multiple myeloma the loss on the lenalidomide and pomalidomide molecules is total and permanent. BMS's oncology franchise is being reconstituted at roughly 60% of its former share of a market that grew about 57%.▪

Price has flipped from tailwind to headwind and is now the binding variable. BMS discloses one aggregate operating driver, the change in U.S. average net selling prices:

Price swung eight points between 2022 and 2025. In 2025 implied U.S. volume and mix still grew and U.S. revenue declined anyway. The industry data corroborate the direction: U.S. brand-name list prices grew 3.5% in 2025 while nominal net prices declined 0.7% and real net prices declined 3.4%, the eighth consecutive year of real net-price decline [web]. BMS's own −4% was worse than the industry's −0.7%, consistent with a Medicare-heavy channel mix.

Three of the six largest revenue lines are now on government-set U.S. prices with different start dates. Adding Opdivo's 2028 exclusivity, 51.0% of FY2025 revenue faces a 2028 U.S. inflection, rising to 58.7% including Orencia. The tariff-relief-for-pricing trade is a new instrument with no precedent to calibrate against; it converts a legislative risk into a contractual one, and the contract is terminable.

Cyclical versus secular: pharmaceutical revenue is not cyclical in the macro sense. BMS's revenue follows the patent cycle, and it has been through one: revenue was $21,244M in 2011 and $15,879M in 2014 at the trough after Plavix and Abilify, and it regained the peak only in 2018, seven years later. The recovery came from one asset that did not exist commercially at the peak, Opdivo, first approved in December 2014.

2026 is a local peak created by the Eliquis list-price cut rather than by demand.▪ Revenue guidance was raised from $46.0–47.5bn to $49.0–50.0bn at the Q2 print, roughly $3bn, driven principally by the Eliquis list-price reduction eliminating accumulated CPI-penalty rebates. Management simultaneously guides a $1.5–2.0bn Eliquis step-down in 2027 and expects EU exclusivity to end in November 2026 with "rapid and steep decline like we have seen with other small molecules outside of the U.S." The peak year is being pulled forward, and the following two years absorb the reversal plus the EU loss plus, in 2028, the U.S. loss on both Eliquis and Opdivo.

Opdivo IV turned negative in Q2 2026 and the gross-to-net series broke. Opdivo IV grew 8% in FY2025 to $10,049M and declined 3% to $2,485M in Q2 2026 with U.S. down 6%. Management attributes it to conversion to Qvantig, and the combined franchise did grow 6.0%, but the franchise growth rate has halved from +10.6% in FY2025. The Q2 2026 results deck also footnotes roughly $200M of sequential inventory build inside the Opdivo line, which if removed puts the underlying rate closer to −11% [estimate: reported $2,485M less the disclosed build, against the implied prior-year quarter]. The gross-to-net series has broken, so the U.S. average-net-selling-price series — the only price KPI BMS publishes — is no longer comparable across the 2025/2026 boundary and the 2026 rebase must be undone before any 2027 price trend can be measured.

What breaks first.

  • Combined Opdivo plus Qvantig growth, already decelerated from +10.6% to +6.0%.
  • Qvantig's share of the nivolumab franchise against the 30–40% target, at 15%.
  • The U.S. average net selling price on a like-for-like basis adjusted for the Eliquis rebase.
  • Growth Portfolio dollars added per year against Legacy dollars lost, +$3,846M and −$3,952M in 2025, which must diverge in the Growth Portfolio's favour from 2027.
  • Reblozyl and Camzyos growth rates, at +29% and +59% in Q2 2026.
  • Cobenfy quarterly revenue, at $63M.
  • Third-party royalty pretax income, which steps down on a disclosed schedule.

7. Critical points

1. Sixty-five percent of revenue loses exclusivity between November 2026 and December 2028, and the replacement block is one-sixth the size of the company. The products losing exclusivity total $31,335M, 65.0% of FY2025 revenue (§3.1). Adjusting for Pfizer's half of Eliquis, the exposure on retained economics is roughly $24bn, about 50%. Against that, the products with a disclosed U.S. exclusivity date beyond 2030 total $7,593M, 15.8% of revenue. AbbVie escaped the same shape with two brands at $6,753M and $2,824M compounding above 39% a year; BMS has to make almost everything work.▪

2. The 2026 revenue and EPS raise comes from a price change on one product, and management's own guidance says it reverses. Guidance moved from $46.0–47.5bn to $49.0–50.0bn and from $6.05–6.35 to $6.75–7.00 in a single quarter. Two lines produced it: Eliquis growth from +10–15% to +20–25%, worth about $1,444M on the FY2025 base, and the Legacy Portfolio decline from −12/−16% to −4/−6%, worth $1,743–2,179M on a $21,785M base, with the two overlapping because Eliquis is inside Legacy. The cause is that BMS cut the U.S. Eliquis list price roughly 40% on 1 January 2026, which removed thirteen years of accumulated CPI-based statutory rebate and the Medicare Part D manufacturer-discount liability. Consolidated gross product sales declined 18% in Q2 2026 while net product sales rose 6%. Management guides a $1.5–2.0bn Eliquis step-down in 2027 off that base.

3. Eliquis is 30% of revenue and about 21% of gross profit, so both the risk and the 2026 upside are roughly a third smaller than the revenue line implies.▪ BMS remitted $6,980M of $14,443M to Pfizer in FY2025, 48.3%, and $44,963M of $94,283M over ten years. Two independent methods put BMS's booked Eliquis gross margin at 48–52% against roughly 79% for the rest of the company. Without the Pfizer share, consolidated gross margin would have been 85.6% rather than 71.1%.

4. The replacement generation is structurally lower-margin than the one it replaces, because of deal structures already signed. Milvexian is an equal profit share with Johnson & Johnson, pumitamig an equal global profit share with BioNTech, and iza-bren a U.S. profit share with SystImmune whose split is not disclosed. Reblozyl already pays Merck 22.6% of net sales, and the Opdivo family pays Ono 4% in North America and 15% elsewhere. Reported gross margin will rise as Eliquis exits — mechanically, because half of Eliquis's cost leaves with its revenue — and then decline again as the partnered assets arrive.▪

5. Roughly $1.76bn of near-100%-margin royalty income disappears across 2026 and 2027. Third-party royalty pretax income was approximately $2.7bn in 2025, 29% of pretax income. The AstraZeneca diabetes royalty of $1,121M terminated on 31 December 2025 and the Keytruda ($588M) and Tecentriq ($47M) royalties terminate on 31 December 2026. The 2027 loss lands in the same year as the guided Eliquis step-down and the same year the two replacement assets read out.

6. Both replacement assets slipped in the same call, and both were framed as encouraging. On 30 July 2026 milvexian's atrial-fibrillation readout moved from late 2026 to Q1 2027 on the pace of events, and the Cobenfy ADEPT programme moved from late 2026 to "early 2027 and be spread across the year" on enrolment pace in ADEPT-2 and ADEPT-4 and slower relapse accrual in ADEPT-1. The Chief Medical Officer said of the milvexian delay, "I see favorably this delay because actually gave us more confidence." Slower event accrual in a blinded non-inferiority safety study is ambiguous; slower enrolment attributed to quality controls is not. The Karuna acquisition that produced Cobenfy was charged $12,122M to acquired IPRD in FY2024.

7. $72.9bn of cash on acquisitions and business development over ten years produced a total shareholder return of 0.9% a year. Over the eight years to end-2025 BMS returned +17.1% against +161% for the pharmaceutical peer group it selects for its own performance graph and +192% for the S&P 500. Over five years to end-2025 it returned +4.8% against the peer group's +98.4%. NOPAT was $8,169M in FY2021 and $8,486M in FY2025. Revenue per share rose 71.6% and free cash flow per share 107% from FY2018.

8. The buyback record is the clearest capital-allocation failure. BMS repurchased 495M shares for $31,230M between 2017 and 2023 at a blended $63.09, against a $64.72 close on 2026-08-07. The largest year was 2022, $8,001M at $73.40, including 30.5M shares bought in October, November and December 2022 at $70.51, $78.23 and $79.98, the highest prices the stock has traded. There have been ten consecutive quarters with no programme repurchase since November 2023, over a window in which the monthly realised price in the Item 5 tables averaged $52.73 and reached a low of $41.24, and the $5,014M authorisation has been frozen since December 2023.

9. The IRA maximum fair price raised BMS's realised Eliquis price rather than lowering it, and the mechanism generalises unevenly. The $231 administered price is 17–31% above BMS's estimated 2025 blended U.S. net realisation of $177–197 per 30-day equivalent, and the accompanying list-price cut removed the accumulated inflation-rebate penalty. Whether that repeats for Pomalyst in 2027 and Orencia in 2028 depends on each product's own accumulated CPI penalty, which is not disclosed. Pomalyst is largely moot regardless: U.S. generics arrived in March 2026 and U.S. Pomalyst revenue was $131M in Q2 2026 against $584M a year earlier, so the government price applies to a stub.

10. The dividend and the balance sheet are fine now and become the constraint later. Net debt declined from $38,470M at end-2024 to $31,656M at 30 June 2026 with leverage at 1.88x on trailing EBITDA, and there are no financial covenants on the notes or the revolver. But H1 2026 operating cash flow was $4,497M against $5,871M, a 24% decline on a 54% increase in pretax earnings, because $3,135M of accrued rebates was paid out. On the H1 run rate the $5.1bn dividend absorbs 67% of free cash flow, the tightest cover since 2016. Contingent milestone obligations of $39.8bn are off the balance sheet against a $44.3bn funded debt stack, and a $6.4bn Celgene contingent-value-rights claim survived a motion to dismiss in December 2025 with no accrual disclosed.

8. Management claim pressure tests

"The Growth Portfolio is the answer to the loss-of-exclusivity cliff." Management leads every call with Growth Portfolio revenue and its share of the total. Two-thirds of that portfolio is not protected past the cliff. Opdivo, Opdivo Qvantig, Orencia and Yervoy total $16,892M, 64.0% of the Growth Portfolio and 35.0% of company revenue; of those, Opdivo and Qvantig ($10,287M) have a disclosed U.S. 2028 date and Orencia and Yervoy have no disclosed U.S. date at all, with Orencia's biosimilar entry now contractually opened and its price government-set from 2028.▪ The post-2030 core is $7,593M, 15.8% of company revenue, growing 34–40% from a base one-sixth the size of the company.

"Subcutaneous Opdivo extends the nivolumab franchise past 2028." On the Q4 2024 call the Chief Commercialization Officer said conversion "will extend the franchise into the 2030s." The FY2025 exclusivity table's footnote (g) assigns Opdivo Qvantig U.S. 2028 and EU 2030, identical to IV Opdivo, "based on the expiry of the COM patent for nivolumab and does not include any potential exclusivity resulting from pending patent applications relating to Opdivo Qvantig." The extension depends on applications that have not been granted. At management's own 30–40% conversion target, at most about $4bn of revenue would be in subcutaneous form when the disclosed protection lapses. Meanwhile the conversion is cannibalising: Opdivo declined 3% in Q2 2026 primarily on conversion to Qvantig, and the combined franchise grew 6.0%.

"BMS is gaining share in immuno-oncology." The 10-K describes the strategy as "extending and strengthening our leadership in IO." BMS's share of the Opdivo-plus-Keytruda revenue pool declined from 28.3% in 2022 to 24.5% in 2025. Keytruda added $6,669M of revenue over FY2023–FY2025 against the Opdivo family's $1,278M, a 5.2x difference in dollar growth from a 2.8x larger base.▪ BMS has also committed $3.5bn of non-contingent cash plus up to $7.6bn of milestones and an equal profit share to license someone else's next-generation immuno-oncology molecule.

"Eliquis delivered demand-driven growth of 21%." The Q2 2026 10-Q filed the same day attributes the increase to "higher demand, foreign exchange impacts of 1%..., and higher average net selling prices in the U.S. In 2026, the Company reduced the list price for Eliquis in the U.S., which resulted in higher realized average net selling prices due to lower rebates." Both demand and price are named and the split is not disclosed. Bounding volume from the disclosed share data puts the price contribution at roughly 18–23 points of the 26.5% U.S. increase [estimate: reported growth less bounded volume growth]. Pfizer's own 10-Q for the same quarter attributes its +21% to "higher net price in the U.S. primarily due to pricing dynamics, including lower rebates and channel mix favorability."

"Falling gross margin means the business is deteriorating." The direction of the mix effect is the opposite of what the headline implies. Consolidated gross margin declines in 2026 because Eliquis, on which BMS earns roughly half of what its revenue line suggests, is guided up 20–25% while Revlimid and Pomalyst at roughly 90–96% gross margin collapse. The constructed Growth Portfolio gross margin is 80–84%. The mechanism reverses after 2028: when Eliquis exits, reported gross margin rises several hundred basis points at the same time as roughly $7.5bn of BMS gross profit disappears.▪

"Management manages the legacy decline better than expected." Management has over-forecast the legacy decline four years running. Revlimid FY2024 was guided at $4.0–4.5bn and delivered $5,773M; FY2025 was guided at $2.0–2.5bn and delivered $2,951M; the Legacy Portfolio was guided at −18% to −20% for FY2025 and delivered −15.4%; and FY2026 was guided at −12% to −16% in February and revised to −4% to −6% in July, a swing worth $1.7–2.2bn.▪ What that does not mean is that erosion is moderating: the July revision came from raising Eliquis, and the ex-Eliquis segment declined 52.8% year over year in the same quarter.

"Business development is rebuilding the franchise." $27,101M of allocated consideration across the four 2022–2024 acquisitions produced three marketed products together annualising below $600M in H1 2026: Cobenfy about $238M, Krazati about $210M, and Augtyro, which is not separately disclosed and is inside a $1,924M line that also holds Onureg, Inrebic, Nulojix, Empliciti and royalties. Seventy percent of the in-process R&D assigned to Augtyro at the Turning Point closing has been written off, and Cobenfy's adjunctive-schizophrenia expansion failed its primary endpoint in April 2025. Against $22.9bn of 2024 consideration, that cohort produced $360M of FY2025 revenue.

"The say-to-do ratio has been embedded in our culture." The claim holds for the annual operating plan and does not hold for the multi-year commitments. Against the November 2021 Investor Day:

Target Promised Delivered
Total revenue CAGR the stated range +2.5%, the bottom of the range
Loss-of-exclusivity decline −$12–14bn −$12,018M, the favourable end
In-line brand growth +$8–10bn +$10,336M, above the top of the range
New product portfolio, 2025 $10–13bn risk-adjusted roughly $7.3–7.6bn, 56–76% of the range
New product portfolio, share of revenue ~25% 15.2–15.8%
Operating margin "low to mid 40s", then ">37%", then "approximately 37%", then unstated 38.5% (FY2024), 38.1% (FY2025), roughly 36% implied for FY2026
Free cash flow, 2021–2023 $45–50bn $39,833M, 11–20% below

The aggregate targets were hit and every composition target was missed.▪

"The long-term case." The commitment has been converted from a revenue number to an asset count. The November 2021 Investor Day put "in excess of $25 billion of revenue potential in 2029" on the new product portfolio and management said "I see 2029 sales higher than 2025 sales." The January 2026 JPM presentation and the February 2026 call give instead "more than 10 new medicines and over 30 meaningful launch opportunities by 2030," with no revenue figure attached. Asked directly on the Q1 2025 call whether trough EPS would stay above $6, the CEO declined the number and pointed to the annual-guidance-only practice.

"The $10 billion debt paydown was completed ahead of schedule." The claim is true on its own terms. The target was set against the 31 March 2024 balance, which was the peak BMS created weeks earlier by issuing $13.0bn of notes to fund Karuna, RayzeBio and Mirati. Net debt at 31 December 2025 of $34,043M is $6,915M higher than at 31 December 2023. The earlier commitment, made twice in 2020, was to under 1.5x debt to EBITDA by 2023 and then by 2024; it is never mentioned again.

Five key inflections:

  • CheckMate-026, August 2016. Opdivo itself did not decline until 2020, which is why the episode is easy to miss. U.S. Opdivo growth went from 37% in 2018 to 2% in 2019, and the FY2019 10-K names the cause as "a smaller previously-treated advanced lung cancer market and increased competition." Total Opdivo went from $7,204M (2019) to $6,992M (2020), the only decline in its life. In 2016 Opdivo was 2.7x Keytruda's size; by 2025 Keytruda was 3.1x the whole Opdivo franchise. In a two-drug oncology class the first credible first-line label is close to permanent.▪
  • Celgene, 2019. Revenue went from $22,561M (2018) to $42,518M (2020) and operating cash flow from $7,066M to $14,052M. It paid out the opposite of the case management made. At announcement Caforio said "this deal is not about Revlimid. This deal is about the short-term launches, the medium- and the long-term optionality of the pipeline." Revlimid delivered $49,726M of revenue over 2020–2025 before declining 77% from its 2021 peak, while the near-term launch portfolio reached roughly $7.3–7.6bn in 2025 against the $10–13bn risk-adjusted target set two years later. The Celgene pipeline did work: Reblozyl, Breyanzi, Zeposia and Abecma went from $286M in 2020 to $4,689M in 2025. The problem was not the price paid for Revlimid. It was that $40,378M of the consideration was equity, permanently raising the share count 24.5%.
  • The targets walked down, then the metric was retired, 2021–2025. The operating-margin commitment moved from "low to mid-40s" (November 2021) to "above 40%" (February 2023) to "our previous operating margin target of at least 37%" (February 2024) to "approximately 37%" (February 2025) to unstated from October 2025. The New Product Portfolio category appeared six times in the FY2022 10-K and ten times in the FY2023 10-K, and zero times in the FY2024 10-K, replaced by "Growth Portfolio," which folds in Opdivo, Orencia, Yervoy and Qvantig — molecules first approved in 2014, 2005 and 2011. The measurement category was removed one year into the target year, before the target could be scored.
  • Boerner, $23bn in a quarter, and the end of the buyback, 2023–2025. Three closes inside ten weeks in a new CEO's first full quarter, funded with new debt, with $12,122M of the $14,027M Karuna purchase price expensed on day one. Buybacks went $8,001M (2022), $5,155M (2023), $0 (2024), $0 (2025). Dividends continued to rise every year. The offsetting cost programme delivered: operating expenses ex-IPRD declined $1.2bn in 2025 and are guided to $16.5bn for 2026.
  • The U.S. price becomes an administered price, December 2025 to January 2026. Three of the four largest revenue lines move to government-set prices on staggered dates. BMS litigated and lost at every level. It then settled on separate terms, trading Eliquis free to Medicaid, seven tons of donated API and roughly 80% direct-to-patient discounts on five brands for tariff relief to January 2029 and exemption from future pricing mandates while the agreement holds. Neither BMS's demand nor its cost position now determines what it collects on 30% of revenue.

How this company behaves. It responds to scientific setbacks with acquisitions, two to three years after the shock: CheckMate-026 in 2016 was answered by Celgene in 2019, and the Revlimid collapse of 2021–2023 by $23bn in ten weeks in Q1 2024.▪ It answers cost pressure with a named productivity programme, and it delivers those: flat opex through 2020, $1.5bn by end-2025 with 2,200 roles, $2.0bn by end-2027, with the 2025 tranche banked. It re-bases the target or retires the metric rather than missing it publicly.▪ It funds shocks by stopping repurchases and never the dividend, which has been paid for 93 consecutive years and raised for seventeen. And it accounts for deals in a way that makes GAAP earnings uninformative: asset-acquisition treatment expensed $11.4bn in 2020 and $12.1bn in 2024 on the day of close.

Episodes the current narrative omits. The $10–13bn 2025 target was never scored publicly and its measurement category was removed. Management has not mentioned Wellington's or Starboard's opposition to the Celgene deal since 2019. The Celgene contingent value right, presented in January 2019 as the mechanism that would "align the interest of Bristol-Myers Squibb and Celgene shareholders," expired unpaid and is in litigation; neither the January 2026 JPM presentation nor the Q4 2025 call mentions it. And the April 2025 Phase III failures were compressed at JPM 2026 into "we had some setbacks on the development side in 2025," without naming either trial.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

10.1 Leadership

Christopher Boerner became CEO in November 2023 and Board Chair in 2024, roughly a year into the job; the 2026 proxy includes a shareholder proposal for an independent chair, which the board opposes. He is an internal commercial executive: head of U.S. Commercial from 2015, international markets from 2017, Chief Commercialization Officer from 2018 and COO in 2023. David Elkins has been CFO since 2019 and came in with Celgene, where he was CFO in 2018–19.

The executive ranks have turned over almost completely in two years. Comparing the FY2023 and FY2025 10-K officer lists, Caforio, Chief Medical Officer Samit Hirawat (replaced effective 1 August 2025, departed 1 November 2025), General Counsel Sandra Leung (in role since 2007), the Corporate Controller and the EVP of Strategy and Business Development have all left. Of the 2024 proxy's six named executive officers, only Boerner and Elkins appear in the 2026 proxy. Hirawat's exit terms included 2025 "All Other Compensation" of $2,625,351 against $289,018 in 2024, and he had bought BMY shares on the open market twice earlier in 2025, about three months before being replaced.

10.2 What management is paid to do

92% of CEO target pay is performance-based and 80% is long-term equity with three-year cliff vesting. Boerner's target total direct compensation is roughly the 40th percentile of the CEO peer set, which the committee attributes to short tenure. Say-on-pay support has been 92–94% for three years. The share-ownership guideline is 6x salary for the CEO, enforced through a retention policy rather than a dated deadline; all directors and executive officers as a group held 1,069,153 shares at 12 March 2026, 0.052% of the company.

The 2025 annual incentive paid 157.66% of target:

Metric Weight 2025 target 2025 actual Payout
Non-GAAP operating income 30% $16,850M $18,484M 187.23%
Growth Portfolio revenue ex-FX 35% $24,850M $26,232M 161.39%
Pipeline (1–5 scale) 25% 3 3.0 100.00%
Sustainability scorecard (1–5) 10% 3 5.0 200.00%
Total 100% 157.66%

Two features of the plan explain the 157.66% payout. Non-GAAP operating income as the plan defines it is computed before the acquired IPRD line: $13,373M in 2024 and $3,721M in 2025, $17.1bn over two years, reduced reported non-GAAP EPS by $6.39 and $1.40 a share and touched the bonus metric not at all. In FY2024, the year of an $8,948M GAAP net loss, the company performance factor was 140.29% and the operating-income component alone paid 138.45%. And Growth Portfolio revenue explicitly "excludes certain key loss of exclusivity brands such as Revlimid, Eliquis, Pomalyst, Sprycel and Abraxane," covering $26,409M of $48,194M. The predecessor metric, In-Line and New Product Revenue, covered 84% of revenue in 2023.

Every material metric change since 2023 replaced a measure BMS was failing with one it was passing. The 2024 plan year replaced non-GAAP EPS with non-GAAP operating income. Total revenue was replaced by Growth Portfolio revenue. The 2025 performance-share grant replaced operating margin with operating income, which removes the penalty a margin metric imposes on revenue bought at a lower margin. A deal's cost never touches the annual bonus or 25% of the performance-share unit; its revenue lands in a metric worth 35% of the bonus and 40% of the unit. There is no ROIC, cash-flow, leverage or per-share metric anywhere in the plan.▪ One counterweight runs the other way: the 2023 EPS metric was measured on a constant share count and the proxy lists neutralising buyback effects as a standing practice, so repurchases were never allowed to manufacture a payout. When the plan moved to operating income in 2024, the last per-share element left the design.

The 2025 operating-income target of $16,850M was 9.3% below the 2024 actual of $18,577M. The 2025 actual of $18,484M was 0.5% below the prior-year actual and paid 187.23%. The committee used downward discretion once, on the pipeline metric: both underlying goal counts came in above the top of their ranges (31 near-term goals against a 25–28 range, 36 long-term against 29–34) and the qualitative overlay scored it at target, against 4.9 the prior year.

The equity plan paid for the shareholder outcome; the cash plan did not. Five-year total shareholder return through 31 December 2025 was +4.8% against the peer group's +98.4%. The 2021–2023 performance-share award paid 65.19% of target with the relative-TSR component at zero (17.1st percentile); the 2022–2024 award paid 63.12% with relative TSR again at zero (15.3rd percentile); one market-share-unit tranche forfeited outright in 2024 and the tranches vesting in 2025 paid 82–93%. The cash plan paid 140.29% and 157.66% across the two years in which the peer gap widened by 46 points.

Candour. Q&A is answered directly and the CEO routinely hands hard questions to the responsible executive. The gross-to-net and IRA disclosure in the filings is unusually explicit, including the mechanical warning that 2026 Eliquis growth is a list-price effect. The 2023 target resets were announced rather than allowed to lapse. Against that: the pattern after a failure is consistent — the word "disappointed" followed immediately by a reframing that denies any consequence ("neither outcome meaningfully alters our strategy or growth trajectory," Q1 2025, on two Phase III misses). And the sharpest disclosure test is Sotyktu. The drug was assigned more than $4bn of 2029 potential in 2021, delivered $291M in 2025, and the fact that BMS has stopped promoting it in dermatology appears only as a footnote on a results slide; management has never said it on an earnings call.

Nine years and $31.2bn of repurchases went in at an average $63.09 against a $64.72 close.▪ The Item 5 tables report the price on shares withheld for tax every month, which gives a monthly realised price series through the whole no-buyback window: the 24 months from July 2024 to June 2026 averaged $52.73 with a low of $41.24 in July 2024. The untouched $5,014M authorisation deployed evenly across those months would have retired roughly 95M shares, 4.7% of the FY2025 diluted count [estimate: authorisation ÷ the mean of the 24 disclosed monthly prices, assuming even deployment and no price impact]. Dividends have been paid for 93 consecutive years and raised for seventeen, and the growth rate has decelerated from about 9% to about 1%: $1.84 (2020), $2.01, $2.19, $2.31, $2.42, $2.49 (2025), $2.52 annualised for 2026. Payout was 39% of free cash flow and 40% of non-GAAP net income in FY2025, and 67% of free cash flow in H1 2026 because operating cash flow declined 23.4%. Management's language on the dividend has not changed with the deceleration.

Stated framework against revealed behaviour. BMS has never stated a hurdle rate, target return or payback threshold for business development anywhere in ten years of transcripts or filings — $72.9bn of cash deployed on external innovation over a decade with no required return published.▪ The CEO's stated filter is qualitative: "it started with making sure that we really like the science." That is a screening description rather than a capital-return test. The one time accountability was addressed directly was the Q4 2024 call: "the senior leadership team of the company owns the decision to move forward with that acquisition… when you're allocating investor capital at that scale, it's critical that senior leaders take ownership and accountability for it." No subsequent call revisits Karuna's returns against that claim.

In 2026 BMS is doing neither. H1 2026 acquisition payments were $156M against $21,821M in FY2024, acquired IPRD $94M against $1,695M in H1 2025, and repurchases zero.

Per-share outcomes against enterprise growth. Taking FY2018, the last clean pre-Celgene year, as the base: over seven years revenue per share rose 71.6% (8.0% a year), free cash flow per share 107% (10.9% a year) and non-GAAP EPS 54.5% (6.4% a year). Chaining BMS's own Item 5 performance graphs, $100 invested on 31 December 2017 was $117.10 at 31 December 2025 against $291.98 for the S&P 500 and $261.11 for the pharmaceutical peer group BMS itself selects; over twelve years from end-2013, $149.00 against $458.98 and $333.60. Per-share fundamentals grew on assets the market discounts: FY2025 free cash flow still depends materially on Eliquis, Revlimid and Pomalyst.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

Bristol Myers Squibb is a serial acquirer that has bought revenue scale successfully and bought future earnings power badly. Celgene more than doubled revenue from $22,561M (2018) to $48,194M (2025) while basic weighted-average shares rose 24.5%, so it reached the per-share line. Everything bought since has not.▪ Of $27,101M of consideration allocated to the four 2022–2024 acquisitions, the three marketed products obtained were together annualising below $600M in the first half of 2026, and 70.1% of the in-process R&D assigned to repotrectinib at the Turning Point closing has already been written off.

BMS has never recorded a goodwill impairment because it routes most deal consideration around goodwill: $32,539M of acquired IPRD was expensed straight to the income statement between 2019 and 2025, of which $23,522M was MyoKardia and Karuna alone, so there is no carrying value left to test.▪ Deal failure shows up as impairment: $6,223M between 2020 and June 2026, plus the $1,830M Inhibitex write-off in 2012 [web] and the total loss of the $1,850M Nektar payment.

Premiums have been at the top of the market in every case where the target was public: 122% for Turning Point, 104% for RayzeBio, 61% for MyoKardia, 54% for Celgene and 53% for Karuna [web].
